title: Stakeholder Management
description: Identify and map stakeholders, assign clear RACI roles, plan communication, and resolve conflicting demands.

questions.prompt: The CFO must approve funding for an internal HR-system upgrade and could stop it, but she has told you she has no interest in the project's details. On a power/interest grid, how should you engage her?

options.text: Manage closely: involve her in all key decisions and working sessions
Keep satisfied: meet her needs with concise updates and consult her on funding issues
Keep informed: send her detailed progress reports to raise her interest
Monitor: minimal effort, since she is not interested in the project

questions.explanation: High power with low interest calls for "keep satisfied": enough engagement that her needs are met, without burying her in detail. Treating her as "monitor" ignores that she can stop the project, and "manage closely" spends effort she has said she does not want.

questions.prompt: A project is replacing the company's customer billing system. The stakeholder register lists the sponsor, Finance, IT, and Sales. Which group is most clearly missing?

options.text: The office facilities team, who maintain the building
The recruiting team, who hire new employees
Marketing's social media team, who run the brand accounts
Customer support agents, who answer customers' billing questions

questions.explanation: Stakeholders include anyone affected by the project's outcome, not only those funding or building it; support agents' daily work changes when billing changes, and they will see problems first. The other groups have no meaningful link to a billing system replacement.

questions.prompt: For the task "Send vendor contract," Legal must review the wording and give feedback before it goes out. Sales only needs to be told once it has been sent. In a RACI matrix, how should Legal and Sales be marked?

options.text: Legal: Responsible; Sales: Consulted
Legal: Accountable; Sales: Informed
Legal: Consulted; Sales: Informed
Legal: Informed; Sales: Consulted

questions.explanation: Consulted means two-way input sought before or during the work (Legal's review); Informed means one-way notification of progress or results (Sales). Legal is not doing the task (Responsible) or answerable for it (Accountable).

questions.prompt: True or false: Once the stakeholder register and engagement plan are approved at project kickoff, they should stay fixed for the rest of the project so the team has a stable reference.
questions.explanation: Stakeholders, their power, and their attitudes change during a project (reorganisations, new regulators, shifting priorities), so identification and engagement planning are repeated throughout (PMBOK 7 Stakeholder Performance Domain). A frozen register goes stale quickly.

questions.prompt: On Tuesday, the PM learns that a vendor delay will push the product launch back four weeks. The weekly status report goes out on Friday. How should the PM tell the sponsor?

options.text: Call or meet the sponsor now with the cause, impact, and options, then confirm in writing
Put it in Friday's status report, since that is the agreed communication channel
Wait until the recovery plan is fully worked out so the sponsor is not alarmed early
Email the full stakeholder list at once so that everyone hears it at the same time

questions.explanation: Significant bad news should reach the sponsor promptly and directly, in a channel that allows questions, with options attached; a written follow-up keeps the record. Letting the sponsor find it in a routine report, or after a delay, erodes trust and wastes decision time.

questions.prompt: A project team grows from 6 people to 10 people. By how much does the number of potential communication channels increase?
questions.explanation: Channels = n(n - 1) / 2: 6 people give 15 and 10 people give 45, an increase of 30. 45 is the new total rather than the increase, and 60 comes from forgetting to divide by 2 (90 - 30).

questions.prompt: Review this RACI matrix. Which row breaks a core RACI rule?

code.source:
Task                 PM   Tech Lead  Sponsor  QA Lead  Ops
Approve budget       R    C          A        I        I
Design architecture  C    A/R        I        C        C
Write test plan      I    C          A        A        I
Production deploy    I    R          I        C        A

options.text: Approve budget, because the PM is Responsible while the Sponsor is Accountable
Write test plan, because it has two Accountable roles and no one Responsible
Design architecture, because one person cannot be both Accountable and Responsible
Production deploy, because Ops cannot be Accountable when the Tech Lead is Responsible

questions.explanation: Each task needs exactly one Accountable person and at least one Responsible; "Write test plan" has two A's and no R, so ownership is unclear. One person holding both A and R is common and valid, as is A and R sitting with different roles.

questions.prompt: Here is the project's stakeholder engagement assessment (levels in order: Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading). Where should the PM focus the most engagement effort?

code.source:
Stakeholder      Influence  Current      Desired
CFO              High       Resistant    Supportive
Facilities mgr   Low        Unaware      Supportive
IT Director      High       Supportive   Leading
Legal counsel    Medium     Neutral      Neutral

options.text: IT Director, because a high-influence champion is needed to lead the change
Legal counsel, because a neutral stakeholder can turn either way
Facilities manager, because the three-level gap is the largest on the matrix
CFO, because high influence combined with active resistance is the biggest threat

questions.explanation: Gap size has to be weighed against influence: the CFO is high-influence and actively resistant, so moving her to Supportive matters most. The Facilities manager has the largest gap, but low influence and mere unawareness are fixed cheaply by informing; Legal is already at its desired level, and the IT Director is already supportive.

questions.prompt: The VP of Sales wants next quarter's capacity spent on a feature for a large prospect; the VP of Operations wants it spent on stability fixes after two outages. Both are high-power stakeholders, there is capacity for only one, and the sponsor owns prioritisation. What should the PM do?

options.text: Lay out both options against the project's agreed objectives and bring the decision to the sponsor
Choose the option the PM judges best, then explain the decision to both VPs afterward
Split the capacity 50/50 so that each VP gets part of what they asked for
Go with whichever VP raised the request first, as the fairest tie-breaker

questions.explanation: When stakeholders with authority conflict, the PM's job is to make the trade-offs explicit (impact, risk, cost, objectives) and get a decision from the person who owns it. Splitting capacity usually delivers neither goal, and deciding alone goes beyond the PM's decision rights.

questions.prompt: The CFO has high power and high interest in your cost-reduction project and is currently resistant. Which engagement tactics are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Meet one-on-one to understand the specific concerns behind the resistance
Involve the CFO in defining the financial success criteria for the project
Reduce contact to a monthly newsletter to avoid further friction
Escalate to the CEO to override the CFO before discussing the concerns
Share draft cost figures before steering meetings so concerns surface early

questions.explanation: High-power, high-interest stakeholders are managed closely: understand their concerns, involve them in the decisions they care about, and avoid surprises in public forums. Pulling back contact or going over their head before engaging usually hardens resistance.

questions.prompt: The PM receives this email three weeks before a fixed-scope launch. Which reply manages the sponsor's expectations best?

code.source:
From: Dana Ruiz (Sponsor)
Subject: SSO for launch?

Hi - can we just add single sign-on to the June 14 launch?
Should be small. Our biggest customer keeps asking for it.
Thanks!

options.text: "Sure, we'll fit it in - the team can absorb a small change like this."
"Sorry, scope is locked for June 14; please raise it for a future project."
"I'll size it by Thursday and bring options: move the date, swap scope, or ship it next."
"We'll add it, and the team will work weekends to protect the June 14 date."

questions.explanation: Acknowledging the request, assessing its real impact, and returning with trade-off options keeps the sponsor in control of the decision while protecting the plan. Saying yes without sizing sets an expectation you may miss, and a flat no ignores a legitimate business need.

questions.prompt: The Head of Compliance, who can block go-live, has skipped four requirement reviews and not replied to review requests, which said "no response by Friday = approval." Build starts next week. What should the PM do?

options.text: Proceed, since the stated deadline means silence counts as formal approval
Meet the Head of Compliance and get explicit sign-off on the key requirements before build
Escalate to the CEO to require the Head of Compliance to attend future reviews
Remove Compliance from the review list to stop delays and keep them informed instead

questions.explanation: Silence from a stakeholder with veto power is not agreement; it is a classic setup for a late rejection at acceptance, when changes cost the most. Getting direct engagement and explicit sign-off now costs little, while escalating first damages the relationship before you understand the reason for the silence.

questions.prompt: Marketing insists on launching September 15 so they can demo at a major trade show. Compliance insists there is no launch until a data-handling audit finishes in November, to avoid regulatory penalties. Both have equal authority. Which approach is most likely to resolve the conflict?

options.text: Escalate and let the sponsor pick one of the two dates
Compromise on a mid-October launch date between the two
Side with Compliance, since regulatory concerns always win
Demo on test data in September; launch after the audit

questions.explanation: Interest-based negotiation (Fisher and Ury, Getting to Yes) looks behind positions (the dates) to interests: Marketing needs a trade-show presence, Compliance needs no exposure of real customer data before the audit. A demo environment meets both; a split-the-difference date fails both, and escalating first skips a solution that may already exist.

questions.prompt: On a cross-functional program, the RACI lists nine roles as Consulted on most design decisions. Decisions now take three to four weeks as drafts circulate for comments. Which change fixes the root cause?

options.text: Limit Consulted to people whose input can change the decision; make the rest Informed
Add a second Accountable role on each decision so approvals can run in parallel
Keep all nine Consulted roles but cap each review cycle at ten working days
Replace the RACI with a weekly all-hands where decisions need full consensus

questions.explanation: Over-consulting is a common RACI failure: every C is a two-way loop that adds delay. Keeping C for people with real expertise or veto and moving the rest to I (one-way updates) speeds decisions without losing needed input. A second A blurs ownership, and consensus by all-hands slows things further.

questions.prompt: You inherit a project whose status reports have been green for eight weeks. The milestone tracker shows 3 of 5 milestones missed, and critical-path tasks are two weeks late. The steering committee meets in three days. What should you do?

options.text: Keep it green until you have a full recovery plan, to avoid alarming the committee
Report red now with the evidence and recovery options, and set objective RAG criteria
Report amber as a middle ground, to soften the change from eight weeks of green
Re-baseline the schedule before the meeting so the milestones are no longer late

questions.explanation: This is a "watermelon" project (green outside, red inside); stakeholders can only decide well with accurate status, and every week of delay narrows their options. Softening to amber or re-baselining to hide performance variance repeats the trust failure that caused the problem.
